title: Extreme Reachability of Continuous Time Random Walks on Networks

problem.claim: Extreme reachability concerns fastest information spreading, quickest search, and earliest arrival in networked stochastic processes.

contributions.claim: Develops a unified short-time framework for extreme reachability of continuous-time random walks on networks.
Derives scaling laws for extreme first-passage times using an instantaneous arrival intensity based on shortest-path contributions.
Proposes an efficient method to compute short-time arrival intensity on large networks.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The many-walker and frequent-resetting limits are reported to be controlled by short-time first-passage asymptotics determined by shortest-path structure and transition rates.
The authors report that the two regimes share the same underlying network quantity.
Predictions are reported as validated on synthetic and real-world graphs.

narrative_sequence.summary: Extreme events determine earliest or fastest outcomes in networked stochastic processes.
The paper develops a unified short-time framework for extreme reachability.
Many-walker and frequent-resetting regimes are linked to short-time first-passage asymptotics, shortest paths, and transition rates.
An arrival-intensity formulation yields explicit extreme first-passage scaling laws and unifies the regimes.
An efficient computation method is proposed and predictions are evaluated on synthetic and real-world graphs.

source_observation.claim: Extreme first-passage behavior is governed by short-time asymptotics involving shortest-path structure and transition rates.

interpretation.claim: For earliest-arrival questions, local shortest-path and rate information may be more informative than long-time diffusion behavior.

application.claim: Analyze fastest spreading, search, or restarting robustness through short-time arrival intensity rather than only long-time diffusion metrics.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this mechanism applies beyond continuous-time random walks or the evaluated graph types.

unknowns: Exact derivations and assumptions behind the scaling laws are unspecified.
The synthetic and real-world graph datasets, baselines, and quantitative validation results are unspecified.
Computational complexity and implementation details of the proposed method are unspecified.
